articles.headline: OFAC Issues Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations, General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related activities. This action aims to disrupt illicit networks that pose a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License to ensure that certain humanitarian and other activities are not unduly impacted. Additionally, an amended Russia-related General License was released, alongside updated Frequently Asked Questions, providing further guidance on existing sanctions programs.

These measures underscore OFAC's ongoing commitment to combating illicit financial activities and adapting its sanctions tools to address evolving threats, while also seeking to minimize unintended consequences for legitimate transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under its counter terrorism sanctions program. These actions target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist organizations and their activities globally.

The designations aim to sever financial and material support networks that enable terrorism, thereby disrupting their ability to plan and carry out attacks. This is part of a broader U.S. government effort to combat international terrorism.

Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated were made available on the Treasury Department's website, emphasizing the U.S.'s commitment to protecting its national security interests.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities for Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Activities
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a new round of designations, targeting individuals and entities involved in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This dual focus highlights the interconnected nature of these illicit networks.

These designations aim to disrupt the financial and operational capabilities of organizations that engage in drug trafficking and support terrorist groups. The U.S. government continues to leverage its sanctions authorities to combat these threats.
The action reinforces the U.S.'s commitment to international security and its efforts to prevent illicit actors from exploiting the global financial system.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation Information
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an update regarding its Iran sanctions program. This update provides additional information and clarifications concerning existing designations related to Iran.

These ongoing adjustments reflect the dynamic nature of sanctions implementation and the U.S. government's continuous efforts to refine its approach to Iranian illicit activities. The update aims to ensure the effectiveness of the sanctions regime.
The Treasury Department's website provides the specific details of this update, which is crucial for entities and individuals engaged in Iran-related transactions to review for compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations. These actions target individuals and entities deemed to be supporting Iran's destabilizing activities.

The designations are part of the U.S. government's ongoing strategy to exert economic pressure on Iran and disrupt its ability to fund activities that threaten regional and international security. This includes efforts to counter Iran's nuclear program, ballistic missile development, and support for terrorism.
These measures aim to further isolate the designated parties from the international financial system and underscore the U.S.'s commitment to addressing the threats posed by Iran.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Issues Cuba Designations and Determination
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a series of new designations, targeting cyber-related threats and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial flows and criminal enterprises operating across borders.

In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also issued new designations related to Cuba, alongside the publication of a Cuba-related determination. These measures reflect the U.S. government's continued focus on addressing various national security and foreign policy concerns.
The designations underscore the U.S.'s commitment to combating cybercrime, transnational criminal activities, and maintaining pressure on the Cuban regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations, Amends Venezuela General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and provided updates to certain existing Iran-related listings. These actions are part of the ongoing effort to counter Iran's illicit activities.

In conjunction with these measures, OFAC published an Iran-related alert to provide guidance and warn against potential evasion tactics. Additionally, an amended Venezuela-related General License was issued, along with a new Frequently Asked Question, offering updated guidance for transactions involving Venezuela.
These steps demonstrate OFAC's adaptive approach to sanctions, aiming to target specific threats while also providing clarity and flexibility for legitimate activities under certain circumstances.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment provides updated guidance and authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are often used to carve out specific activities from broader sanctions, aiming to mitigate unintended humanitarian impacts or facilitate certain types of legitimate trade. The details of this amended license are crucial for compliance.
This action reflects OFAC's continuous review and adjustment of its sanctions programs to ensure they remain effective and appropriately targeted.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo-related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions aim to address illicit activities in both regions.

The North Korea designations are part of ongoing efforts to counter the regime's weapons of mass destruction programs and other destabilizing actions. The DRC-related designations target individuals and entities contributing to conflict and human rights abuses in the region.
These measures underscore the U.S.'s commitment to using sanctions as a tool to promote peace, stability, and human rights globally.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
